title: Every assumption, and what it costs
lede: This is the page that argues with the other fourteen. Every result in this series rests on assumptions, most of them stated in a footer and then not returned to. Here they are collected, broken one at a time, and priced.
claims: jumps cap the improvement below 2.1x on four more runs
worst jump path loses about three times the premium

chapters.title: The ledger
chapters.dek: Nine assumptions, and the page of this series that measured what each one is worth.

figures.title: What the model assumes, and what it costs
figures.caption: The right-hand column is the useful one. Every entry is a measured number from a page in this series rather than a general warning — which is the difference between knowing a model has limits and knowing where they bind.

figures.title: Break one assumption at a time
figures.caption: With every assumption intact the hedge is close to perfect: the error spreads by 5.8% of the premium. Hedging once a day instead of eight times widens it to 15.2%; switching vol to 8.9%; fat tails to 11.4%. Costs barely widen it but move the whole distribution down, 11.9% of the premium, every time. Jumps are in a class of their own: a 43.1% spread, and a worst path that loses three times the premium. Break all five and the spread is 49.3%. The ledger's entries are not equal, and the one the hedge cannot touch at all is the one that dominates.

checks.q: Which failing assumption breaks the argument rather than just adding a cost?
checks.right: Jumps. Costs make the replication expensive; a discontinuous path makes it impossible, because the hedge cannot adjust during a move that takes no time
checks.why: Jumps. Every other item on the list leaves the replication argument intact and charges you for it. A jump means the delta hedge is set for a price the stock is no longer at, with no opportunity to correct, so the position is genuinely unhedged over exactly the move that matters. That is a difference in kind, and chapter 02 measures it.

terms.Fat tails: More of the distribution's variance coming from rare large moves than a lognormal allows. It is a statement about shape, and it is compatible with any variance you like.

chapters.text: Black–Scholes is usually introduced as a formula and criticized as a philosophy. Neither is very useful. What is useful is a list of the specific things it assumes, and a number attached to each — because the assumptions do not fail equally, and knowing which ones are expensive is most of what separates using a model from believing it. The table below is that list. Almost every line has already been measured somewhere in this series, which is the point: the failures are not vague, they have magnitudes. Three deserve highlighting because their cost is larger than people expect. Continuous trading. Page 13 showed that adding transaction costs turns "hedge as often as possible" from a theorem into a corner solution that is wrong — the objective becomes a U-curve with a minimum around 128 rehedges on a ninety-day option. Continuous paths. This is the assumption chapter 02 breaks, and it is the most damaging on the list because it invalidates the replication argument itself rather than merely adding a cost to it. Constant volatility. Page 07 measured a delta difference of 0.097 — about ten shares a contract — arising purely from which sticky convention you assume, with identical prices on the screen. What the table also shows is that the assumptions are not independent. Jumps produce fat tails ; fat tails produce a smile; a smile makes "the volatility" ambiguous; the ambiguity makes delta model-dependent. Most of this page is one failure propagating. What the model assumes, and what it costs Severity The right-hand column is the useful one. Every entry is a measured number from a page in this series rather than a general warning — which is the difference between knowing a model has limits and knowing where they bind. The ledger is a list. Here it is as a machine. A short at-the-money call is delta-hedged on 300 paths, first in the world the model assumes, then with whichever assumptions you choose to break. The outline is the perfect world; the bars are yours. The table on the right is what each broken assumption costs by itself. Break one assumption at a time Break With every assumption intact the hedge is close to perfect: the error spreads by 5.8% of the premium. Hedging once a day instead of eight times widens it to 15.2%; switching vol to 8.9%; fat tails to 11.4%. Costs barely widen it but move the whole distribution down, 11.9% of the premium, every time. Jumps are in a class of their own: a 43.1% spread, and a worst path that loses three times the premium. Break all five and the spread is 49.3%. The ledger's entries are not equal, and the one the hedge cannot touch at all is the one that dominates. Trader's lens Risk managers rank the model's assumptions by what breaking them costs, because that tells them where to spend: more frequent hedging and cheaper execution fix the small ones, and nothing in the delta hedge fixes a jump. Gap risk is managed with position size, with options bought in the wings, or by not being short gamma into events. Hedging frequency trades error against cost; past a point more hedging only pays the broker. Costs are a mean, not a spread: they show up as steady underperformance. Jumps are a tail, not a mean, and only options or size control them. Rule of thumb: if one scenario on your book loses several times the premium, that scenario, not the greeks, is your risk.

chapters.title: The hedging error stops falling
chapters.dek: Page 01's headline result is a theorem about continuous paths. Introduce jumps and more hedging buys almost nothing.

figures.title: Hedging error against rebalance count
figures.caption: The lower panel is the test and the upper one is the consequence. A flat diagnostic means every doubling of effort buys the full √2; a rising one means you are paying for improvement you are not getting. Set the jump intensity to zero and the vermilion trace lies down on the blue one.

checks.q: Your desk doubles its hedging frequency and the realized hedging error barely improves. What does that tell you?
checks.right: That the residual is dominated by gaps rather than by discretization. You are already past the point where more trading helps, and you are now paying page 13's costs for nothing
checks.why: You have hit the jump floor. This is a genuinely useful diagnostic: plot your realized error against rebalance frequency and see whether sd × √N is flat. If it rises, extra hedging is buying less than the theory promises, and the right response is to stop trading more and start thinking about the tail — which usually means buying options rather than shares.

chapters.text: Page 01 sold a call, delta-hedged it mechanically, and measured what was left. The answer was clean and it is worth restating precisely: the standard deviation of the hedging error falls like 1/√N , so the residual can be made as small as you like by trading often enough. The figure reproduces that. Under pure diffusion, the standard deviation falls from 2.90 at eight rebalances to 0.535 at 256 — and the diagnostic quantity sd × √N stays flat, 8.2 at eight rebalances and 8.6 at 256, which is what a clean 1/√N law looks like. Now turn on jumps: one expected jump a year, averaging −12%. Everything else identical. The standard deviation now falls from 3.50 to 1.85 — and stops. The diagnostic climbs from 9.9 to 29.7 , which means the error is no longer falling like 1/√N. It is approaching a floor , and the floor is the jump risk, which no amount of rebalancing can touch because the whole point of a jump is that you do not get to trade during it. Put as a single comparison: going from 8 rebalances to 256 — thirty-two times the trading — buys you a 5.4× reduction in error under the model, almost exactly the √32 = 5.66 the theory predicts. In the jumpy world it buys 1.9× . These are the figure's opening run of 900 paths per point; press for another run and they move by a few percent. You have paid thirty-two times the transaction costs of page 13 for a third of the benefit. That is the most important practical consequence in this series. The instruction "hedge more often" is derived from an assumption, and in a market with gaps it stops paying long before it stops costing. Where exactly it stops is an empirical question about the underlying, which is why hedging frequency is a desk-level judgement rather than a formula. [equation: sd(error) · √N = constant (diffusion) sd(error) → floor (with jumps)] Reads as: under continuous paths the error shrinks without limit as you trade more; with jumps it converges to something you cannot hedge away. The diagnostic is the product — flat means the law holds, rising means it does not. Hedging error against rebalance count The diagnostic: sd × √N, flat if the law holds The experiment The lower panel is the test and the upper one is the consequence. A flat diagnostic means every doubling of effort buys the full √2; a rising one means you are paying for improvement you are not getting. Set the jump intensity to zero and the vermilion trace lies down on the blue one. Try this Set jump intensity to zero. Predict what the diagnostic panel does, then turn jumps up to three a year and predict again. Derivation — why a jump cannot be hedged and a diffusion can Over a small interval, a delta-hedged position's P&L is the part the hedge misses — the curvature times the square of the move. [equation: P&L ≈ ½ Γ (ΔS)²] Reads as: what survives the hedge is gamma multiplied by the move squared. This is page 01's gamma rent. Under diffusion, ΔS over an interval of length dt scales like √dt , so (ΔS)² scales like dt — and summing N of them gives a total that converges as N grows. Shrinking the interval shrinks the uncertainty in the sum, which is the 1/√N law. A jump does not scale with dt at all. Its size is drawn from a fixed distribution regardless of how short the interval is, so (ΔS)² is O(1) rather than O(dt), and shrinking the interval does not shrink it. [equation: diffusion: (ΔS)² ~ σ²S² dt jump: (ΔS)² ~ J²S², independent of dt] Reads as: you can outrun a diffusion by trading faster and you cannot outrun a jump, because the jump does not get smaller when you do. So the error decomposes into a piece that vanishes with more hedging and a piece that does not. The second piece is the floor in the figure. Where it breaks. The simulation uses a single jump size and intensity, which is a caricature — real gaps cluster, arrive with warning some of the time, and have a size distribution that is itself uncertain. The direction of the result is robust and the level is a parameter. Note also what is not claimed: the jump risk is unhedgeable with the underlying , but it is perfectly hedgeable with other options, which is the entire reason the wing of a surface has the shape page 07 described.

chapters.title: Fat tails, at exactly the same variance
chapters.dek: A smile is not evidence that the market disagrees about volatility. It is evidence that it disagrees about shape.

figures.title: Two distributions with identical variance
figures.caption: The upper panel is two densities you would struggle to tell apart by eye, with identical variance by construction. The lower panel is what the option market does with the difference. Set the two regime volatilities equal and the smile flattens to a line — the smile is entirely a statement about the mixture, not about the level.

checks.q: A market shows a pronounced smile. What is the minimum you can conclude?
checks.right: That the implied distribution is not lognormal. It could have exactly the variance the at-the-money option implies and still smile, purely from having fatter tails
checks.why: Only that the distribution is not lognormal. Variance and shape are separate facts, and a smile is a statement about the second. This is why page 11 warns against reading a variance strike above the at-the-money vol as a forecast — it is largely the shape being averaged into a single number.

terms.Mixture: A distribution built by drawing from one of several regimes. The simplest way to produce fat tails while holding total variance exactly fixed.

chapters.text: The lognormal is not wrong about how much stocks move. It is wrong about how that movement is distributed between ordinary days and extraordinary ones — and that distinction is invisible in a variance number. Here is the cleanest demonstration. Build a world where 85% of the time volatility is 18 and 15% of the time it is 42 . The total variance of that mixture is exactly the variance of a single volatility of 23.238% . Same variance. Different shape. Now price options in both worlds and invert to implied volatility. The mixture produces 25.27% at the 70 strike, 22.00% at 90, 21.60% at the money, 22.11% at 120 and 22.87% at 130 — a smile, with its minimum near the money and both wings lifted. Read that again, because it is the point. Nobody changed the variance. Nobody expressed a view about the level of volatility. A perfectly ordinary fat-tailed distribution with the same second moment produces a smile on its own. Which reframes the whole of page 07 . The smile is not primarily the market saying "volatility is higher than you think out there". It is the market saying "the distribution has more weight in the tails than a lognormal does", and the only way to say that in Black–Scholes' vocabulary — which has one parameter — is to quote a different parameter at each strike. The single-volatility model's errors are correspondingly structured rather than random. Priced at the variance-matched 23.238%, it overprices the body — 10.67 against the mixture's 10.03 at the money — and underprices the far left tail , 0.380 against 0.566 at the 70 strike. A desk short the body and long the wings against that model is systematically, not occasionally, mispriced. chapters.title: What one volatility costs on a real surface
chapters.dek: Price a skewed market at the at-the-money volatility and the errors run from −74% to +213%.

figures.title: Market prices against a single-volatility model
figures.caption: The upper panel's two curves look close because the axis is dominated by the in-the-money options. The lower panel is the same information in the units that matter, and it does not look close at all — it crosses zero once, near the money, which is the only place anyone checks.

checks.q: Why does a single-volatility model survive in production despite these errors?
checks.right: Because it is accurate where it is checked. The at-the-money error is about 2%, and that is the option everyone looks at — the large errors are in the wings, which are cheap and rarely reconciled
checks.why: It is right where anyone looks. The errors do not cancel — they are systematically one sign below the money and the other above, so a book with any directional option position accumulates them. This is the general shape of model risk: not that a model is wrong everywhere, but that it is right in the region used to validate it.

chapters.text: Chapter 03 explained why a surface exists. This chapter prices the mistake of ignoring it — which is a mistake people make less often deliberately than by inheritance, from a spreadsheet or a risk system with one volatility field per underlying. Take a market quoting a skewed surface: 25 at the money over six months with a −0.30 skew, which is unremarkable for an equity index. Price the whole chain at the at-the-money volatility instead and compare. At the 75 strike the market pays 1.0296 and the flat model says 0.2689 — the model is low by 74% . At 85 it is low by 40% . At the money the error is a tolerable 2% . And then it inverts: at 115 the flat model is 46% high , and at 125 it is 213% high — pricing an option at more than three times what the market will pay. Three things follow. The error is not noise, it is a shape. It is systematically negative on the downside and positive on the upside, so a book that is long puts and short calls will be marked wrong in the same direction every single day. A random error averages out over positions; this one accumulates. The worst percentage errors are on the cheapest options. The 213% error is on an option worth 0.37, so the dollar mistake is small — until it is a large position, which is exactly what cheap wing options tend to be. The at-the-money option is fine. Which is precisely what makes the practice survive: the model is validated where it is checked, and wrong where nobody looks. chapters.title: What survives
chapters.dek: Every assumption fails and the model is still the right thing to use. Both halves of that sentence are load-bearing.

figures.title: How much of the risk each layer actually removes
figures.caption: Delta hedging removes most of the risk and leaves a floor; hedging the wing with other options reaches under the floor, because the jump risk that is unhedgeable with shares is perfectly hedgeable with options. That is the honest summary of what the model does and does not buy you.

checks.q: Given everything on this page, what is implied volatility actually for?
checks.right: Quoting. It is a change of units that makes prices comparable across strikes, expiries and underlyings — a shared denominator that works even though everyone knows the model behind it is false
checks.why: It is a quoting convention. That sounds deflationary and is the opposite — a common language for price is enormously valuable, and it does not require the model generating it to be true. The whole surface is then the market's correction, which is why "use Black–Scholes with a surface" is a coherent position rather than a contradiction.

chapters.text: Fourteen pages built on a model, and this one has spent four chapters breaking it. The obvious conclusion — that the model should be replaced — is wrong, and understanding why is the last thing this series has to say. The model is a language, not a description. Nobody believes volatility is constant. Quoting an option in implied volatility is not a claim that the model is true; it is a change of units that makes prices comparable across strikes, expiries and underlyings. A 3.40 option and a 12.10 option cannot be compared; a 23 vol and a 31 vol can. The model's job here is to be a shared denominator, and a wrong model does that job perfectly well as long as everyone uses the same wrong model. The failures are mapped. That is what the surface is . The market has taken the model's inadequacy and priced it strike by strike, so the quoted surface contains exactly the information the model omits. Using Black–Scholes with a surface is not using a broken model; it is using the model as an interpolation scheme with the corrections supplied by the market. The hedging argument survives in the direction that matters. Chapter 02 showed the error has a floor, not that hedging is pointless — at 256 rebalances the jumpy world's error is still 1.85 against an unhedged position's many multiples of that. Delta hedging removes the first-order risk exactly as advertised. What it cannot remove is the part that was never first-order. And the alternatives inherit the same problem. Stochastic volatility, jump-diffusion and local volatility models all fit better and all contain parameters that must be estimated from data that is short, noisy and non-stationary. A more flexible model is not automatically a more accurate one; it is a model with more ways to be confidently wrong. So the working position is neither belief nor rejection. Use the model, quote in its units, take the surface as the market's correction to it, and keep an explicit list of the places where it is not merely imprecise but structurally silent — jumps, liquidity, financing and the behavior of other people. That list is this series, and its most useful property is that every entry has a number next to it. That is the honest summary of what the model does and does not buy you.

chapters.title: Check yourself
chapters.dek: Six questions across the page, and the series.

checks.q: Thirty-two times the hedging frequency buys how much error reduction?
checks.right: About 5.4× under pure diffusion — near the √32 = 5.66 the theory predicts — and only about 1.9× once jumps are present
checks.why: 5.4× under the model, 1.9× with jumps. The theory's own prediction is √32 = 5.66, so the diffusion case confirms page 01 almost exactly. The jump case is where "hedge more often" stops paying while continuing to cost.

checks.q: Why can't a delta hedge remove jump risk?
checks.right: Because a jump's size does not shrink as you shorten the rebalancing interval. Diffusive moves scale like √dt, so trading faster shrinks them; a jump is the same size however fast you trade
checks.why: The jump does not get smaller when you trade faster. Unpredictability is not the issue — diffusive moves are unpredictable too, and they hedge fine. The issue is scaling: (ΔS)² is proportional to dt for a diffusion and independent of it for a jump.

checks.q: A mixture of an 18 vol regime and a 42 vol regime has the same total variance as a single 23.2 vol. What do options do?
checks.right: They smile. Implied vol runs 25.27% at the 70 strike down to 21.60% at the money and back up to 22.87% at 130, with the variance unchanged throughout
checks.why: They smile, at identical variance. This separates two ideas that get conflated constantly: how much the stock moves, and how that movement is distributed. A smile is a statement about the second.

checks.q: Pricing a skewed chain at the at-the-money volatility. Where are the errors largest in percentage terms?
checks.right: In the wings. The at-the-money error is about 2%, while the 125 strike is overpriced by 213% and the 75 strike underpriced by 74%
checks.why: The wings, by a wide margin. And the errors have opposite signs either side of the money, so they accumulate on any directional book rather than canceling. The model is accurate exactly where it gets checked.

checks.q: If every assumption fails, why keep using the model?
checks.right: Because it works as a quoting language and the market supplies the corrections through the surface. A shared denominator does not need to be true to be useful
checks.why: It is a language with market-supplied corrections. The failures are not small — this page measured several of them at tens of percent. What makes the model workable is that the surface encodes precisely what the model omits, so using it with a surface is an interpolation scheme rather than an act of faith.

checks.q: Jump risk cannot be hedged with the underlying. What can hedge it?
checks.right: Other options. A jump is a large move in the underlying, which is exactly what a wing option pays for — which is also why the wings of a surface are priced the way page 07 describes
checks.why: Other options. The unhedgeability in chapter 02 is specifically with respect to shares . This is the connective tissue of the whole series: the wing is expensive because it insures something shares cannot, and someone short it is being paid for exactly the risk the model says does not exist.
